summary: Provides general information about Proxy-PAR (PNNI Augmented Routing), a mechanism that lets routing information flow between IP routers and ATM networks. It is an informational memo, not a standard, and its text is mostly general background.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a short introduction to a helper that lets Internet routers and ATM networks share information about who can be reached.

questions: what is proxy-par pnni augmented routing
subtitle: A simple way for IP routers to register services and discover peers through ATM networks.

tldr.problem: ATM-attached IP devices want to discover and interact with other devices over an ATM cloud without implementing the full complexity of PAR (PNNI Augmented Routing).
tldr.mechanism: Proxy-PAR provides a lightweight client-server protocol where clients register the protocols they support (OSPF, BGP, etc.) and their IP addresses, while servers flood this information through the PNNI routing hierarchy.
tldr.outcome: IP devices can automatically discover and establish connectivity with peers across ATM networks, enabling protocols like OSPF to scale across ATM peer groups without manual configuration.

facts.label: Model
facts.value: Client initiates all operations; server never pushes

today: RFC 2843 is an Informational memo describing Proxy-PAR, a simplified version of PAR for service discovery in ATM networks. It enables IP routers and other non-ATM devices to register and discover services over an ATM cloud using the PNNI routing hierarchy.

sections.title: Proxy-PAR: simple service registration for ATM
sections.content:
Proxy-PAR is a minimal version of PAR (PNNI Augmented Routing) that allows non-ATM devices—particularly IP routers—to use the PNNI (Private Network-Network Interface) hierarchy to discover and announce services without implementing the full PAR specification. PNNI is an ATM routing protocol that organizes networks into peer groups and routing levels.

The protocol uses a simple client-server model where the client side is much simpler than the server side, allowing fast implementation on existing IP devices. Instead of pushing information to clients, the server provides a flooding mechanism so clients can register their own services and query for services registered by others. The main advantage is automatic discovery: devices can learn about each other across an ATM cloud without manual configuration or a central registry server.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is an older network technology. This tool lets computers on an ATM network ask each other what they do (like "I run OSPF") and then find each other automatically, using the ATM network's built-in way of spreading that information.

sections.title: How Proxy-PAR registers and queries services
sections.content:
The protocol consists of two main parts: the Hello protocol and the registration/query protocol. The Hello protocol establishes and maintains a Proxy-PAR adjacency between a client and server, similar to the PNNI Hello protocol. Hellos traveling from server to client inform the client about the lifetime the server assigns to registered information, so the client knows when to refresh.

Once an adjacency exists, a client registers the protocols it supports by sending registration messages to the server. Each registration includes a VPN ID, an IP address, subnet mask, the protocol type (OSPF, BGP, etc.), and an abstract membership scope that maps to a PNNI routing level. The server floods this information through the PNNI network according to the scope, so all peers at that level and above learn about the service.

The client obtains information by sending query messages requesting services within a specific VPN, scope and IP address prefix. The server never pushes information to the client; the client is responsible for periodic queries and re-registration to keep its view current. This simplifies the protocol but assumes clients do not request large amounts of data and that services are relatively stable.
sections.plainLanguage: A router says to the ATM server: "I run OSPF on address 1.1.1.1 in subnet 1.1.1/24." The server tells all the other ATM switches so other routers can ask: "Who runs OSPF in subnet 1.1.1/24?" and the server tells them this router does.

sections.title: Membership scope and PNNI hierarchy
sections.content:
A key feature of Proxy-PAR is the use of membership scope to exploit the PNNI routing hierarchy. When a client registers a service, it associates an abstract scope (such as "local" or "local+1") with it. The server maps this scope into a PNNI routing level that controls how far the information is flooded in the network hierarchy. This allows different protocols to be announced at different levels: OSPF, for example, might be advertised only within a peer group, while BGP could be advertised globally across peer-group boundaries.

The Proxy-PAR server also provides filtering based on VPN IDs and IP address prefixes, supporting Virtual Private Networks. A network provider can configure a server so that clients are restricted to specific VPN IDs, preventing devices in one VPN from discovering devices in another. Because each VPN represents a completely separate IP address space, this provides VPN isolation while still allowing automatic service discovery within each VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: The ATM network has levels: some switches are close by, others are far away. A router can say "announce me locally" or "announce me to the whole company," and the server makes sure the right group of switches learns about it. This also keeps different VPNs separate so they cannot accidentally find each other.

sections.title: Security and protocol interoperability
sections.content:
Proxy-PAR itself does not define security mechanisms beyond VPN filtering; it relies on the security features of PNNI. Discovered protocols have their own authentication: for example, when two routers discover each other through Proxy-PAR as OSPF neighbors, they authenticate using OSPF's built-in authentication when they establish the OSPF session. Thus, even if a Proxy-PAR query returns a wrong peer, authentication will fail.

Proxy-PAR can interoperate with ILMI (Interim Local Management Interface) based server discovery; a PAR-capable device can register services with ILMI so both mechanisms work together. The protocol supports many IP protocols including OSPF, BGP, RIP, EGP, IS-IS, MARS, NHRP and ATMARP, with optional additional protocol-specific information (such as OSPF area ID or BGP AS number) that is not used in filtering but is passed through for the client to interpret.
sections.plainLanguage: The ATM network is responsible for keeping VPNs separate and secure. Once routers discover each other, they use their own protocols to authenticate, so a router cannot trick another into becoming its peer. This lets Proxy-PAR be simple and safe at the same time.
